Reference: Barkoczy, S. (2017). Foundations of Taxation Law (9th ed.). Oxford University Press, Australia. Page no. 269, Chapter 11.   Chapter 11: Income from personal exertion (Page 269)In this chapter the courts have looked at the income from personal exertion to include remuneration from employment and rewards received for services rendered. In the case of Brent v FC of T 71 ATC 4195 it was held that a person who gave a guarantee for a loan to a company of which he was a director and shareholder, and received a commission in respect of the loan, was not assessable on the commission under an income tax legislation. input: Given question: Which of the following fringe benefit is taxable? Option A: De minimis benefit Option B: Benefits that are given to supervisory employees Option C: Benefits provided to rank and file employees Option D: Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan Option E: Benefits given to support employees education The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Fringe benefits tax regime is essentially a tax on a wide range of benefits provided by an employer to an employee. This tax is payable by the employer, not the employee, because the benefit is received from the employment. There are a number of different types of fringe benefit, which all fall within these two categories.In this case, the fringe benefit is taxable because it falls within one of these two categories. A de minimis benefit is a minor, trivial benefit that can be given to an employee without it being classified as a fringe benefit. It is called a de minimis benefit because the value of the benefit is so small that it is unimportant. In practice, de minimis benefits are usually related to the workplace, such as a birthday cake or a cup of coffee. They are not subject to FBT because they are not significant enough to constitute a benefit.A benefit that is given to supervisory employees is also taxable. These benefits are treated differently under the FBTAA because they are given to employees who have some level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits provided to rank and file employees are also taxable. These benefits are generally given to employees who do not have any level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan are also taxable.An employer may provide an employee with a range of benefits from which the employee chooses the benefit that best suits the employee’s needs. For example, an employee might be able to choose between an additional week of annual leave and a one-off payment of $5000.The option e is the correct answer because it supports employees education. This is a taxable fringe benefit. Employers are encouraged to provide educational assistance to their employees because it helps to increase the skill levels of the workforce and improve productivity. However, if an employer pays for an employee to undertake a course of study, the benefit will be regarded as a taxable fringe benefit.  * Chapter 20, Fringe Benefit Tax, Foundations of Taxation Law (9th Edition), Stephen Barkoczy, 2017. source: Topic 8 Lecture Slides - Fringe Benefit Tax - Page 17 of 26 - Notional deduction slides. Some of the taxable fringe benefits are as follows:De minimis benefit: A de minimis fringe benefit is a fringe benefit that has a taxable value of less than $300. Only one de minimis benefit is exempt from FBT each year, regardless of the number of employees. This exemption applies to any fringe benefit that satisfies the de minimis test. The test is satisfied if the taxable value of the fringe benefit is less than 2% of the total gross wages paid by the employer to all its employees in the year of tax. The de minimis benefit is also subject to a limit of once per employee each year.Benefits that are given to supervisory employees: A fringe benefit is not an exempt benefit if it is provided to a supervisor (as defined in s 136(1)) unless the benefit is also provided to a non-supervisory employee.Benefits provided to rank and file employees: A fringe benefit is not an exempt benefit if it is provided to a rank and file employee (as defined in s 136(1)) unless the benefit is also provided to a non-rank and file employee.Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan: These benefits are taxable fringe benefits. However, they are exempt benefits if they are provided by a person who provides insurance or a retirement benefits plan to the public.Benefits given to support employees education: These benefits are taxable fringe benefits unless the employee is on a study break.  Tax Invoices and Adjustment Notes.  
Entities are required to hold tax invoices and adjustments notes at the time they lodge their GST returns for a relevent tax period in order to be able to claim input tax credits and decreasing adjustments for the period (s 29-10(3), s 29-20(3) GSTA).  
It is important to note that entities must be able to produce tax invoices and adjustment notes for expenditure on request by the Commissioner.  
Further, entities must be able to produce evidence to support a claim for input tax credits or decreasing adjustments.  
Documentation should be kept for a period of five years in order to facilitate any potential tax audits.  
Source: Barkoczy, S. Foundations

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Mr. Chauree is now 62 years old and paid $ 400,000 to buy an annuity of $20,000. The annuity is payable on annual basis for the remaining period of his life. Mr. Chauree's life expectancy factor be 24 years. On his death. a total amount of $100,000 will be paid to his wife. How much is Mr. Chauree required to show in his assessable income annually? Option A: $12,500 Option B: $16,666 Option C: $12,000 Option D: $12,800 The correct answer is Option A.
reference: 12,500 - Annual amount required to be shown in assessable income = A(B-C)/D                               = (1($400,000 - $100,000))/24                               = $12,500 Where, A = taxpayer's share of annuity in relation to the year of income B = amount of the undeducted purchase price of the annuity C = residual capital value in relation to the annuity or nil D = relevant number in relation to the annuity (Barkoczy, 2017, p308) Topic 5 (Chapter 11)Statutory IncomeReference:Barkoczy, S. Foundations of Taxation Law 2017, (9th edition), Oxford University Press Australia.CSU LAW505 MODULE, TOPIC 5, Statutory Income.
best_explanation: Mr. Chauree is required to show in his assessable income annually the following amount: $20,000 - ($400,000 x 10/24) = $12,500. The formula is based on the following: Deductible amount = A(B-C)                                     DA = the taxpayer's share of the annuity in relation to the year of incomeB = the amount of the undeducted purchase price of the annuityC = the residual capital value in relation to the annuity or nil (where such amount does not exist)D = the relevant number in relation to the annuity (life expectation of the annuity) (Barkoczy, 2017, p 308) Topic 5 (Chapter 11)Statutory IncomeReference:Barkoczy, S. Neither of these gains are discount capital gains or eligible for small business concessions. John also made a capital loss of 10,000 on the sale of his land and has a net capital loss carried forward from the previous year of 6,000. What is his net capital gain that must be included in his assessable income? Option A: $20,000 Option B: $16,000 Option C: $ 38,000 Option D: $22,000 Option E: None of the above The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 20,000 - 10,000 = 10,000 (CG to be included in assessable income) 10,000 + 6,000 (Net capital loss brought forward from last year) = 16,000 (Net Capital Gain) Note: Capital losses can be applied against capital gains to reduce the overall taxable capital gain. In this case, the net capital gain is reduced by the capital loss. "CGT events" chapter 19 - page 475 Textbook. Topic 6 - Capital Gains TaxBarkoczy, S. best_explanation: Unlike cash income, capital gains are not generally taxed until they are realized, that is, until a taxpayer disposes of the capital asset that has produced the gain. Capital gains can be either short-term or long-term.  Capital gains are computed by comparing the sale price of the capital asset with its cost. The gain is the difference between the two amounts. Capital losses can be used to offset capital gains. If the capital loss is more than the capital gain, the excess can be applied against other capital gains or against the net capital loss of the previous year. If the capital loss is a short-term capital loss, it can be applied only against a long-term capital gain.  In the given case, John made 30000$ capital gain on the sale of shares and 8000$ capital gain on the sale of units. He also made a 10000$ capital loss on the sale of his land but this loss is not able to apply against these capital gains because these gains are not capital losses. So, the net capital gain that must be included in John's assessable income is 0$. But, the net capital loss from previous year is 6000$ and this can be applied against these capital gains. So, the net capital gain that must be included in John's assessable income is 20000$ and it can be calculated as 30000$ capital gain - 6000$ net capital loss. input: Given question: Functions of AASB (Australian Accounting Standards Board) under s.227 of ASIC Act, includes the followings, EXCEPT, Option A: Promoting financial stability by leading institutions to manage risk prudently for minimizing losses to depositors, policy holders etc. Option B: Developing a conceptual framework Option C: Contributing for developing a single set of accounting standards for global use Option D: Formulating accounting standard that consist of law under s.334 of the Corporations Act Option E: Uplifting the significance of main objects of the financial reporting system part of the ASIC Act The correct answer is Option A.
reference: 1- Promoting financial stability by leading institutions to manage risk prudently for minimizing losses to depositors, policy holders etc. - This is the core objective of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). 2- Developing a conceptual framework - The AASB develops conceptual frameworks for the purpose of accounting for transactions and events. 3- Contributing for developing a single set of accounting standards for global use - The AASB works towards achieving this objective through its involvement in the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). 4- Formulating accounting standard that consist of law under s.334 of the Corporations Act - The power to formulate accounting standards is vested in the AASB by s.227(1) of the ASIC Act. 5- Uplifting the significance of main objects of the financial reporting system part of the ASIC Act - The main object of the financial reporting system is to assist in the economic decision making process.The above are the functions of the AASB under s.227 of the ASIC Act, except for point 1 as it is the core objective of the ASIC. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which one is not considered as 'non-assessable non exempt income' ? Option A: Registered charities (s 50-5 ITAA97) Option B: Foreign source income of a temporary resident (s 768 - 910 ITAA97) Option C: Genuine redundancy payments (s 83-170 ITAA97) Option D: Demerger dividends (s 44(4) ITAA36) The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Refer to textbook chapter 12 page 316 for more on this topic. According to the textbook, register charities are considered as 'non-assessable non-exempt income' under s 50-5 ITAA97.  Chapter 12 - Exempt Income and Non-Assessable Non-Exempt Income – Page # 316 – 319 – Twenty-Fifth Edition – 2017 by Stephen Barkoczy.  ​Registered Charities (s 50-5 ITAA97)A registered charity (eg a body approved under the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Act 2012) is a 'non-assessable non-exempt income' entity (s 50-5 ITAA97). This means that the organisation must include in assessable income all amounts that are received from providing its services, unless the amount is an 'exempt income' or 'non-assessable non-exempt income' (Barkoczy, 2017, p 316).Foreign source income of a temporary resident (s 768 - 910 ITAA97)This provision provides that a temporary resident (a resident for tax purposes of a foreign country) is not taxable in Australia on any income (including income from Australian sources) that is derived before the individual becomes a resident of Australia (Barkoczy, 2017, p 316).Genuine redundancy payments (s 83-170 ITAA97)A payment is a genuine redundancy payment if it is a one-off payment and meets certain conditions (Barkoczy, 2017, p 316).Demerger dividends (s 44(4) ITAA36)Where a company distributes, within 12 months of each other, capital that has been used to reduce shareholders' entitlements (or both capital and assets), then the recipient shareholders may be subject to income tax as though they had received a dividend (Barkoczy, 2017, p 316).References:Barkoczy, S. Foundations of Taxation Law 2017, (25th edition), Oxford University Press Australia.CSU LAW505 MODULE, TOPIC 10, Topic 10 - Exempt Income and Non Assessable Non Exempt Income.CSU Interact.CSU LAW505 MODULE.CSU. best_explanation: Registered charities (s 50-5 ITAA97) is a 'non-assessable non-exempt income' income.  Foreign source income of a temporary resident (s 768 - 910 ITAA97) is a 'non-assessable non-exempt income'.  Genuine redundancy payments (s 83-170 ITAA97) is a 'non-assessable non-exempt income'.  Demerger dividends (s 44(4) ITAA36) is a 'non-assessable non-exempt income' income.  A 'non-assessable non-exempt income' is an income that is stated to be a 'non-assessable non-exempt income' in the income tax legislation and is not included in assessable income.  Exempt income is an income on which you don't need to pay tax.  Therefore, Answer A is the correct answer.  Reference: Barkoczy, S. input: Given question: As per the s 23-5, Which of the following two requirements are needed to satisfy an entity to register for GST ? Option A: The entity’s GST turnover is below  the ‘registration turnover threshold’ Option B: The entity carries on an ‘enterprise' Option C: The entity’s GST turnover is over the ‘registration turnover threshold’ Option D: b and c Option E: None of the above. The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 1) An entity must “carry on an enterprise”: This requirement is derived from the Australian tax law concept of an “enterprise” which is defined in s 9-20 GST Act as “a business, profession, trade, employment, vocation or calling, but does not include a recreational pursuit or entertainment”. In Ruling TR 92/3, the Commissioner has indicated that the term “entertainment” should be interpreted restrictively and that an activity will not be entertainment if it contains a sufficient degree of pleasure or enjoyment to be regarded as a recreational pursuit. 2) The entity’s GST turnover is over the ‘registration turnover threshold’: The registration turnover threshold is $75,000 ($150,000 for non profit organisations).An entity may register for GST even if its GST turnover is below the registration turnover threshold if it carries on an enterprise. However, entities that carry on an enterprise must register for GST regardless of their turnover unless they are employees or certain other exclusions under Div 33. input: Given question: Which case illustrated the difficulty when distinguishing between annuities and installment payments for the fixed price of a capital asset? Option A: Smith v FCT 87 ATC 4883 Option B: FCT v Holmes 95 ATC 4476 Option C: Payne v FCT 96 ATC 4407 Option D: Australia and New Zealand Savings Bank Ltd v FCT 93 ATC 4370 Option E: IRC v Ramsay [1953] 1 All ER 847 The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The principle established by the Ramsay case has been followed in several subsequent cases. In FCT v Holmes 95 ATC 4476, it was held that where a taxpayer enters into an agreement to make periodic payments to another entity, the critical question is whether the payments are consideration for a transferable right to receive income or capital. In contrast, in Smith v FCT 87 ATC 4883, the court found that a lump sum payment with no conditions attached was a capital payment, even though there was some evidence of an intention to return the payments as an annuity. Similarly, in Payne v FCT 96 ATC 4407, the court held that a one-off payment was a capital payment, again because there was no condition attaching to the payment. By contrast, Australia and New Zealand Savings Bank Ltd v FCT 93 ATC 4370 involved a loan agreement which required the borrower to repay the loan in equal monthly instalments over a period of years. The agreement also contained a provision entitling the bank to require the borrower to immediately repay the loan if the borrower breached any of the other provisions of the agreement. It was held that the payments were part of the purchase price of the house and therefore capital in nature. best_explanation: IRC v Ramsay [1953] 1 All ER 847 illustrated the difficulty when distinguishing between annuities and installment payments for the fixed price of a capital asset. In this case, the taxpayer entered into an agreement to sell his house for 15000 pounds and to purchase a house for 15000 pounds. The contract provided that the taxpayer would make equal monthly payments over a period of 19 years. The payments represented the equivalent of the rent of the house which the taxpayer could have received if he had elected to lease the house rather than purchase it. The payments were held to be an annuity and the taxpayer was assessed as having sold the house for its then market value. reference: be used to overcome the deficiencies in the legislation. It helps in filling the legislative vacuums. Judicial precedent, also known as stare decisis, is the principle that courts should follow their own previous decisions. This allows for consistent interpretation and application of the law. Taxation law is no exception to this principle. It is interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent. This means that judicial precedent is an important source of tax law. Legislation may be incomplete or ambiguous. In such cases, the courts can refer to the legislative history, which includes things like the reports of parliamentary committees, to help fill legislative vacuums. This process of interpreting legislation involves consideration of a number of factors, including the words of the legislation, the purposes behind it and the intended beneficiaries. When interpreting legislation, the courts often look at the purpose behind it. They do this by considering the words of the legislation in the context of the problem it was designed to address. They also consider the intended beneficiaries of the legislation. Reference is taken from chapter- 1 ,Research design and methodology, Taxation principles and theory. (8th edition), Stephen Barkoczy, Oxford University Press Australia and New Zealand. It is therefore essential that the legislation is interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent to ensure that taxpayers can rely on the law. Tax law recognises the value of money and therefore provides that expenses are immediately deductible while capital outgoings are deductible over time. This is because capital outgoings are spread over a period of time to ensure that the taxpayer is not disadvantaged by having to pay tax on the cost of a capital item in the year in which it is acquired.Gains and losses are generally computed by comparing the amount with the taxpayer’s “cost” of the CGT asset. reference: ........................... is the answer.A taxpayer's assessable income includes not only amounts that are ordinary income but also amount that are statutory incoe (s 6-10(1) ITAA97).Ordinary income: These are the income which are earn through ordinary sources so that it easy to identify and calculate the amount of tax.Statutory income: These are the income which are specified in tax legislation so that it is difficult to identify and calculate the amount of tax.For example: Dividend income, Royalty income, Capital gains etc.Topic 2 - Lecture Slides 4 & 5. (Reference: Barkoczy, S. Foundations of Taxation Law 2016, (8th edition), CCH Australia Page No: 12.1 and 12.2) (12.1) Assessable income for a tax payer is the sum of Ordinary income and Statutory income. (12.2) The assessable income include income from business, dividends, royalties and capital gains. All these all are part of the taxable income. (Taxable income = Assessable income - Deductions) (Barkoczy, S. Foundations of Taxation Law 2016, (8th edition), CCH Australia Page No: 13.1 and 13.2) (13.1) The gross assessable income is the assessable income minus deductions. (13.2) The net assessable income is the remaining amount after deducting the total deductions from the gross assessable income. (Barkoczy, S. (14.2) The non-resident individual tax rate in Foundation of taxation 2016 page 206. ( Reference: Barkoczy, S. Foundations of Taxation Law 2016, (8th edition), CCH Australia )
